Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] The Gentlemen internal recon via Advanced IP Scanner · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] The Gentlemen: internet-facing assets exposed to the group's known-exploited edge/BYOVD CVEs · [LLM] The Gentlemen BYOVD: ThrottleStop.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys load & GentleKiller EDR-killer drivers (CVE-2025-7771) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — No Manners Here: The Ruthless Rise of The Gentlemen Ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] The Gentlemen 'gentlemen*' scheduled task creation/execution · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] The Gentlemen C2: SystemBC / Go backdoor beacon to actor infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] The Gentlemen anti-forensics: wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs · [LLM] The Gentlemen impact prep: Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic · [LLM] The Gentlemen encryptor execution by known SHA256/SHA1 hash · [LLM] The Gentlemen mass file encryption — .umc16h extension write/rename burst · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
The Gentlemen: internet-facing assets exposed to the group's known-exploited edge/BYOVD CVEs AIExploitation High
Scopes hosts carrying the specific n-day and BYOVD vulnerabilities The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) is documented exploiting for initial access and SYSTEM escalation. This is a prioritisation/exposure hunt, not a behavioural detection, so it runs against vulnerability inventory rather than telemetry. Rationale: Uses the five CVEs the Unit 42 article explicitly lists as known-exploited by The Gentlemen for initial access (FortiOS CVE-2024-55591, Erlang/OTP SSH CVE-2025-32433, SMB client CVE-2025-33073, React2Shell CVE-2025-55182) and privilege escalation (ThrottleStop.sys CVE-2025-7771), joined to internet-facing status to rank remediation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/gentlemen-ransomware-vulnerable-driver-security-gear • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped/decommissioned hosts flagged as vulnerable but not reachable from the internet
  • Compensating controls (virtual patching/WAF) already mitigate the CVE on the edge device
  • TVM inventory lag showing a device as vulnerable after a patch was applied out-of-band
  • Third-party appliances where the CVE'd component is not the exploitable service
Suppression filter
| where IsInternetFacing == true or isempty(IsInternetFacing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort results by IsInternetFacing=true and severity; confirm the vulnerable service is actually exposed (external scan / firewall rule). 2) Contain: emergency-patch or virtually-patch the exposed edge devices (Forti/Erlang SSH/SMB/React2Shell) and disable ThrottleStop.sys via Microsoft vulnerable-driver blocklist. 3) Hunt: for any confirmed exposed host, pivot to auth logs for anomalous successful logons post-exposure and to the other Gentlemen UCs (gentlemen* task, GentleKiller driver load).

| where CveId in ("CVE-2024-55591","CVE-2025-32433","CVE-2025-33073","CVE-2025-55182","CVE-2025-7771")
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate) by DeviceId, DeviceName, CveId
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, IsInternetFacing, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId

The Gentlemen 'gentlemen*' scheduled task creation/execution AIInstallation High
Hunts the group's signature scheduled tasks whose names begin with the string 'gentlemen', used to launch their Go payloads. This is the single most article-specific execution artifact and is safe to alert on because the token is unique to the actor. Rationale: Directly implements the article's explicit recommendation to alert on any scheduled task matching 'gentlemen*'; the token is unique to the actor so false positives are near-zero, warranting an alerting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal application or admin legitimately using 'gentlemen' as a task-name substring (rare)
  • Security team creating a hunting/canary task named gentlemen* for testing this very rule
  • Backup or RMM software with an unrelated task coincidentally containing the token
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full task XML and the parent process; note the action/binary the task launches and its signer. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the task, and quarantine the referenced payload binary. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same task name and for the GentleKiller driver load, wevtutil log clears, and encryptor hashes from the other UCs; check for lateral spread from this host.
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence = ProcessCommandLine, Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
 (DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where FolderPath has @"\System32\Tasks\"
  | where FileName startswith "gentlemen"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Evidence = FolderPath, Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "gentlemen")
    or (EventID == 4698 and EventData has "gentlemen")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = coalesce(SubjectUserName, Account), EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen Ransomware 'gentlemen' Named Scheduled Task
id: 2f4b9d1a-6c7e-4a83-9c11-8ab0e7d54f21
description: Detects creation or execution of a scheduled task whose name/command contains the actor-unique string 'gentlemen', used by The Gentlemen (Storm-2697) RaaS to launch payloads.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'gentlemen'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*schtasks.exe OR *SchTasks.exe OR *SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*gentlemen* OR *Gentlemen* OR *GENTLEMEN*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/gentlemen/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Endpoint.Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.user Endpoint.Processes.process Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Endpoint.Processes.process="*gentlemen*" by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.user Endpoint.Processes.process Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
The Gentlemen BYOVD: ThrottleStop.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys load & GentleKiller EDR-killer drivers (CVE-2025-7771) AIExploitation High
Detects the group's Bring-Your-Own-Vulnerable-Driver escalation via the ThrottleStop driver (renamed ThrottleBlood.sys) exploiting CVE-2025-7771, plus the GentleKiller framework's other abused kernel drivers. Kernel load of these named drivers on a business endpoint is a high-fidelity precursor to EDR tampering. Rationale: Anchors on CVE-2025-7771/ThrottleStop.sys named in the article and the corroborated ThrottleBlood.sys rename plus the GentleKiller driver set from ESET's IOC repo; kernel load of these on an enterprise host is inherently malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc/blob/master/gentlemen/README.adoc • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/gentlemen-ransomware-vulnerable-driver-security-gear
ATT&CKT1068 T1211 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate ThrottleStop CPU-tuning install on an enthusiast/engineering workstation loading throttlestop.sys
  • Anti-cheat drivers (vgk.sys, dmx.sys) loaded by installed games on user machines — excluded from this list to reduce noise
  • Security lab / red-team detonation of the driver in a sandbox
  • Vendor driver with a coincidentally similar short name (e.g. eb.sys)
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "ThrottleStop.sys" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\ThrottleStop")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that loaded the driver and its signer; confirm the host is not a known ThrottleStop legitimate user. 2) Contain: isolate the host, add the driver hash to the Microsoft vulnerable-driver blocklist / WDAC, and preserve memory for kernel-tamper analysis. 3) Hunt: check DeviceProcessEvents for the GentleKiller executables (Allpatch2.exe, All.exe), EDR tamper/uninstall events, and subsequent wevtutil log clears and encryptor execution on the same host.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ThrottleStop.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","havoc.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys","dmx.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 6
| extend ImageLoaded = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).DataItem.EventData.Data[4]["#text"])
| where ImageLoaded has_any ("ThrottleStop.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","havoc.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ImageLoaded
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen anti-forensics: wevtutil clearing Security/System event logs AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the actor clearing the Windows Security or System event logs with wevtutil, a defense-evasion step the article explicitly recommends alerting on. Interactive log clearing on a server or workstation is rare and high-signal. Rationale: Implements the article's explicit behavioural-alert recommendation for wevtutil clearing Security/System logs; the machine-account exclusion and log-name predicate keep it high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1070.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually clearing logs during troubleshooting or before a maintenance window
  • Log-management tooling that rotates/clears channels via wevtutil
  • Golden-image build / sysprep processes clearing logs before capture
  • Compliance scripts clearing logs on a schedule
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("logrotate.exe","sysprep.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\Sysprep")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the clearing account is an authorised admin and whether a change ticket exists; capture the parent process. 2) Contain: if unauthorised, isolate the host and preserve any forwarded/SIEM-side copies of the cleared logs. 3) Hunt: on the same host, look back (before the clear) for GentleKiller driver loads, the gentlemen* task, shadow-copy deletion, and encryptor hashes to reconstruct the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "wevtutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Security","System")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "wevtutil.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("cl ","clear-log") and CommandLine has_any ("Security","System"))
    or (EventID == 1102)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = coalesce(SubjectUserName, Account), EventID, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: The Gentlemen wevtutil Security/System Event Log Clearing
id: b7d3f602-1a48-4c9e-8b25-3f6a9c0e77d4
description: Detects use of wevtutil to clear the Security or System event log, an anti-forensics step used by The Gentlemen ransomware.
references:

detection:

      - 'clear-log'
  selection_log:

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*wevtutil.exe OR *WevtUtil.exe OR *WEVTUTIL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*cl* OR *clear-log*) @CommandLine:(*Security* OR *System*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/wevtutil\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(cl\s|clear-log)/i
| CommandLine=/(Security|System)/

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process_name=wevtutil.exe (Endpoint.Processes.process="*cl *" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*clear-log*") (Endpoint.Processes.process="*Security*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*System*") by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.user Endpoint.Processes.process Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)`
The Gentlemen internal recon via Advanced IP Scanner AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects execution of Advanced IP Scanner (including renamed copies, via file metadata) which the actor uses for internal network mapping before lateral movement. Matching on Famatech product/company metadata catches renamed binaries the actor may drop. Rationale: Directly uses the article's named tool (Advanced IP Scanner) for discovery; matching on Famatech/product metadata makes it resilient to renaming, which ransomware affiliates commonly do. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://redpiranha.net/news/the-gentlemen-ransomware-analysis
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/network admins legitimately using Advanced IP Scanner for inventory
  • MSP or helpdesk tooling that bundles the scanner
  • Penetration testers / vulnerability-assessment runs
  • Renamed but benign copies flagged only on metadata
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("rmm_agent.exe","screenconnect.clientservice.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the executing user is IT/network staff and whether the run is on their normal workstation vs a server/DC. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the host and capture the scan output artifacts. 3) Hunt: correlate with bursty internal SMB/RDP connection fan-out from the same host and with the gentlemen* task or GentleKiller activity to confirm an active intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("advanced_ip_scanner.exe","advanced_port_scanner.exe")
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Advanced IP Scanner"
    or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Famatech"
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "advanced_ip_scanner.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "advanced_ip_scanner.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "advanced_port_scanner.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Advanced IP Scanner Execution (The Gentlemen Discovery)

The Gentlemen C2: SystemBC / Go backdoor beacon to actor infrastructure AICommand & Control Low
Surfaces outbound connections to the three IPs the article attributes to The Gentlemen's SystemBC / custom Go backdoor C2. NOTE: these IPs are single-source (Unit 42 article only) and were NOT found in ESET's IOC repo, so this ships as a hunting watchlist pending independent validation. Rationale: Uses the three C2 IPs from the article's pre-extracted IOCs paired with SystemBC attribution; confidence is Low and tier hunting because a WebFetch of ESET's Gentlemen IOC repo did not list these IPs — treat as single-source until corroborated by current threat intel. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc/blob/master/gentlemen/README.adoc
ATT&CKT1071 T1090 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The IP has been reassigned to a benign hosting tenant since the article (IPs churn)
  • Shared bulletproof/VPS ranges where a neighbouring IP is legitimate
  • Security tooling / threat-intel enrichment services that themselves connect to the IP for analysis
  • A researcher sandbox deliberately beaconing to the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the IP against a live threat-intel feed (ThreatFox/OTX) and identify the initiating process — SystemBC often runs from a Go binary in a temp/user path. 2) Contain: block the IP at the firewall/proxy and isolate any host that connected. 3) Hunt: on connecting hosts, pivot to the Go backdoor process, the gentlemen* task, GentleKiller driver loads, and any subsequent shadow-copy deletion / encryption.

The Gentlemen impact prep: Volume Shadow Copy deletion via vssadmin/wmic AIActions on Objectives High
Detects deletion of Volume Shadow Copies with vssadmin or wmic immediately preceding encryption, an anti-recovery step the article explicitly recommends alerting on. Excludes machine/service accounts to keep it high-fidelity. Rationale: Implements the article's explicit recommendation for behavioural alerts on vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion; command-token predicates plus machine-account exclusion make it low-FP for a ransomware pre-encryption step. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/other backup software running snapshot pre-cleanup
  • Sysadmin manually managing shadow storage during troubleshooting
  • Disk-imaging / migration tooling deleting stale snapshots
  • SCCM/DISM servicing operations that touch VSS
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","veeam.backup.manager.exe","beremote.exe","vsnapvss.exe","dismhost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process and account; a shadow delete parented by an unusual binary (not a backup product) is highly suspicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately — shadow deletion is typically minutes before encryption; verify offline backups are intact. 3) Hunt: sweep for the .umc16h encryption burst and encryptor hashes across the environment and for the gentlemen* task on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete" and ProcessCommandLine has "shadow")
    or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("shadowcopy","delete"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has "delete" and CommandLine has "shadow")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Gentlemen encryptor execution by known SHA256/SHA1 hash AIActions on Objectives Medium
High-fidelity detection for execution (or write) of the specific C/Go encryptor binaries by their published hashes. Pure IOC match — safe to alert. Rationale: Pure IOC match on the four SHA256 and four SHA1 encryptor hashes from the article's IOC block; hash matches are unambiguous, warranting a critical alerting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/ • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc/blob/master/gentlemen/README.adoc
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Deliberate detonation of the sample in a malware-analysis sandbox reporting to the same EDR tenant
  • Threat-intel/AV vendor test hosts
  • Extremely rare hash collision (effectively impossible for SHA256)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host and whether execution succeeded vs was blocked by AV/EDR; identify the parent and drop path. 2) Contain: isolate immediately, kill the process, and disable the account it ran under; verify backups. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for these hashes, the .umc16h extension burst, shadow-copy deletion, and the C2 IPs to size the blast radius.

The Gentlemen mass file encryption — .umc16h extension write/rename burst AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the encryption stage by a rapid burst of files gaining the corroborated '.umc16h' extension from a single process, thresholded to fire only on bulk activity. Complements the hash-based UC by catching encryptor variants whose hash isn't yet known. Rationale: Uses the '.umc16h' encrypted-file extension surfaced in secondary vendor reporting on The Gentlemen, thresholded per-process/5-minutes so it fires on the encryption burst rather than a single stray file; catches unknown-hash variants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/the-gentlemen-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application coincidentally producing many '.umc16h' files (extremely unlikely — non-standard extension)
  • Backup/restore of an already-encrypted victim dataset repopulating .umc16h files
  • Forensic tooling copying evidence files that retain the extension
  • Bulk file-server operation on a directory that already contains encrypted artifacts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess and folder(s) affected; confirm whether files are being newly created (active encryption) vs copied. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host and any file server it is writing to, and revoke the account. 3) Hunt: pivot to the encryptor hashes, shadow-copy deletion, gentlemen* task, and GentleKiller driver load; check other hosts for the same extension burst to scope propagation.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".umc16h"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleProc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), SamplePath = any(InitiatingProcessFolderPath), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50   // 50 = bulk-encryption burst threshold in a 5m window
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".umc16h"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleProc = any(ActingProcessName), SampleCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50   // 50 = bulk-encryption burst threshold in a 5m window
| order by FileCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:*.umc16h
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.umc16h$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=FileCount))
| FileCount > 50
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name="*.umc16h" by Endpoint.Filesystem.dest Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Filesystem)` | where count > 50
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name="*.umc16h" by Endpoint.Filesystem.dest Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Filesystem)` | where count > 50
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

detection:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase

    - attack.execution

       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "51b9f246d6da85631131fcd1fabf0a67937d4bdde33625a44f7ee6a3a7baebd2", "025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "8ae6bd18b129061f63642531f1b684cf0383c75d", "d605994fc72a2bb59b5cfb1624a1b9170eca73a2", "5aa3124e5c4921e5edfc60133b5d71da21b07da3", "a5cf917ec4a7dfbdfa43621398604805d860c718"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] TSDProxy management-API auth bypass: spoofed x-tsdproxy-id replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TSDProxy internal auth token (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) captured/handled in host process command line
TSDProxy internal auth token (x-tsdproxy-auth-token) captured/handled in host process command line AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the TSDProxy internal per-process secret header 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token' appearing in any process command line on a host running tsdproxy or a proxied backend. This header is injected server-side into upstream requests only and must never surface in a shell; its presence in process telemetry indicates a compromised backend has captured the token to replay against the management API (GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8). Rationale: 'x-tsdproxy-auth-token' is a unique internal-only header constant (consts.HeaderAuthToken) that TSDProxy sets exclusively on server-to-backend requests; it should never appear in a user-space process command line, making its presence a near-zero-FP signal of token capture. Anchored directly on the advisory PoC's token-exfiltration step. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy • https://medium.com/@sylvesterranjithfrancis/authentication-at-the-edge-the-identity-aware-proxy-pattern-and-the-one-header-that-gets-you-633cc2b6a2d2
ATT&CKT1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer inspecting or debugging forwarded proxy identity headers on the host
  • CI/integration test harness that echoes or asserts on request headers
  • A monitoring/health-check script that dumps HTTP request headers from the backend
  • TSDProxy verbose/debug logging that echoes request headers into stdout captured as a process arg
Suppression filter
// Exclude known CI/ops accounts that legitimately inspect headers
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("ci-runner","monitoring")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host runs tsdproxy or a backend it proxies; pull the full process tree and parent (InitiatingProcess) — a web/app service account spawning curl/wget/python handling this header is high-confidence compromise. 2) Contain: treat the TSDProxy auth token as burned — upgrade to >= 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e and restart tsdproxy to regenerate the per-process token; isolate the backend host. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 for replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/, and review tsdproxy management activity for proxy restart/pause, config enumeration, and outbound webhook deliveries (SSRF).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "x-tsdproxy-auth-token"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TSDProxy management-API auth bypass: spoofed x-tsdproxy-id replay to 127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for the exploitation step of GHSA-g936-7jqj-mwv8: a localhost request carrying an attacker-controlled 'x-tsdproxy-id' identity header to the TSDProxy management API (127.0.0.1:8080, /api/v1/ paths). The management server trusts x-tsdproxy-id from localhost once a valid forwarded token is presented, so this pattern is the privilege escalation to full admin control (enumerate proxies, restart/pause services, trigger webhook SSRF). Rationale: Combines the spoofed-identity header 'x-tsdproxy-id' (attacker-supplied per the PoC: 'x-tsdproxy-id: attacker') with the fixed management endpoint 127.0.0.1:8080 / /api/v1/proxies from the advisory. Legitimate management calls arrive over Tailscale, not as a localhost request forging the identity header, so the combination is a high-fidelity escalation signature. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/almeidapaulopt/tsdproxy • https://medium.com/@sylvesterranjithfrancis/authentication-at-the-edge-the-identity-aware-proxy-pattern-and-the-one-header-that-gets-you-633cc2b6a2d2
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin manually calling the local management API from the host for ops/troubleshooting
  • Local health-check or readiness probe hitting /api/v1/ on 127.0.0.1:8080
  • CI/automation that enumerates proxy config against the management port
  • A load test or debugging session that manually injects x-tsdproxy-id to test identity handling
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","ci-runner") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","curl","wget","python","python3")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process/account — a proxied backend service account (not an interactive admin) issuing a loopback request to 127.0.0.1:8080 with a forged x-tsdproxy-id is confirmed exploitation; capture the id value and target /api/v1 path. 2) Contain: rotate the TSDProxy token by upgrading to >= 1.4.4-0.20260603142855-434819b4421e and restarting; block backend egress to the management port (network-namespace/firewall). 3) Hunt: review management-API actions in the same window for proxy restart/pause (DoS), full proxy enumeration, and configured-webhook deliveries (SSRF); correlate with UC1 token-capture hits on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "x-tsdproxy-id"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("127.0.0.1:8080","localhost:8080","/api/v1/")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS-to-RCE via nodeIntegration)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Out-of-band write to SiYuan attribute-view store (data/storage/av/*.json payload plant)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SiYuan Electron renderer spawns shell/LOLBin (stored-XSS-to-RCE via nodeIntegration) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-50551/CVE-2026-54158: a stored XSS payload in an attribute-view cell fires in SiYuan's Electron renderer, which runs with nodeIntegration:true and reaches require('child_process') to spawn arbitrary host commands. SiYuan is a note-taking app and should never parent cmd/powershell/wscript, so any such child is high-fidelity RCE. Rationale: Uses the exact article-named parent binary (SiYuan.exe) and the nodeIntegration→child_process RCE chain; a knowledge-management Electron app spawning interpreters is near-zero baseline, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory DB (CVE-2026-54158) and the SiYuan GitHub security advisories confirming the same nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false config across the CVE family. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.007 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan community plugins that legitimately shell out (e.g. export-to-PDF, git-sync, or pandoc integration plugins invoking node/cmd)
  • Developers running SiYuan from source spawning node.exe during build/watch
  • SiYuan auto-updater launching a helper/installer process on version upgrade
  • Security tooling injecting into or wrapping SiYuan.exe and inheriting the parent name
  • conhost.exe host allocation appearing as a benign child on interpreter launch
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "conhost.exe") | where not (FileName =~ "node.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--build","electron","webpack"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and grandchild tree on the host; benign plugin activity has recognisable args (pandoc, git, node build), whereas RCE shows encoded PowerShell, downloaders, or discovery commands. Confirm SiYuan version < 3.7.0 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the SiYuan process tree, and quarantine the user's workspace `data/storage/av/*.json` files before they re-sync to other devices. 3) Hunt: enumerate every device sharing that user's SiYuan sync/workspace (this bug fires on every peer that opens the poisoned row), review those hosts for the same SiYuan.exe child-process pattern and any outbound C2 from the spawned child.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SiYuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","node.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\SiYuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe",@"\powershell.exe",@"\pwsh.exe",@"\wscript.exe",@"\cscript.exe",@"\mshta.exe",@"\rundll32.exe",@"\regsvr32.exe",@"\certutil.exe",@"\bitsadmin.exe",@"\curl.exe",@"\node.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Out-of-band write to SiYuan attribute-view store (data/storage/av/*.json payload plant) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence/plant stage of CVE-2026-50551: the malicious attribute-view cell is written to data/storage/av/<avID>.json and rides workspace sync to every peer. A process other than SiYuan.exe writing to that exact store path indicates manual/malware staging of the payload or an external sync client propagating a poisoned AV file. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact backing-store path data/storage/av/<avID>.json plus the fact that only SiYuan.exe should author those files; a foreign writer surfaces manual PoC-style plants and malware staging the poisoned AV JSON. Corroborated against the SiYuan GitHub advisory and GitLab Advisory DB confirming the storage path and sync-propagation model. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54158/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-50551/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party sync clients (Dropbox.exe, OneDrive.exe, Syncthing.exe, Resilio) writing the workspace JSON — note these are ALSO the legitimate payload-propagation vector, so triage rather than blanket-exclude
  • Backup/restore software (Veeam, Duplicati, robocopy) copying the workspace into place
  • User manually restoring a workspace snapshot or migrating between machines
  • Antivirus/EDR remediation rewriting the file after a scan
  • Text editors or scripts a power-user runs to bulk-edit their own SiYuan database
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","Syncthing.exe","ResilioSync.exe","robocopy.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the written data/storage/av/*.json and grep the cell content for HTML breakout patterns (</textarea>, "><img, src=x, onerror=, <script); a benign SiYuan AV file contains none. Identify the writing process — if it is a sync client, treat as propagation and pivot to origin. 2) Contain: quarantine the offending JSON, block the SiYuan sync channel for the affected workspace, and prevent peers from opening the block-attribute panel until cleaned. 3) Hunt: on every device sharing that workspace, look for the paired RCE signal (UC: SiYuan.exe spawning cmd/powershell/node) and confirm all endpoints are upgraded to SiYuan >= 3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where FileName endswith ".json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("SiYuan.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\storage\av\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".json"
| where ActingProcessName !has "SiYuan.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth pre-auth RCE: filebrowser spawns shell/recon commands (CVE-2026-54088) AIExploitation High
Hunts the File Browser server binary (`filebrowser`) spawning a shell or OS discovery/tooling child process. Under CVE-2026-54088 an unauthenticated attacker injects shell metacharacters into the login username/password, which `os.Expand` substitutes unsanitised into the admin's hook-auth command, causing the `filebrowser` process to execute attacker OS commands. A file server should essentially never spawn `id`/`whoami`/`curl`/`wget`, so any such child is high-fidelity. Rationale: Uses the concrete vulnerable binary name `filebrowser` (parent) plus the article's PoC injection primitive (shell metacharacters `;`/`$(`/backtick and `id`/`whoami` running under the hook command). A file-server process spawning recon/OS tooling is near-zero in benign operation. Cross-checked against filebrowser.org auth docs and auth/hook.go on GitHub. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1033 T1087.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately configured a hook-auth command that shells out to an external auth backend using curl/wget (e.g. validating against an LDAP/OIDC gateway)
  • Custom container entrypoint or healthcheck wrapper also named 'filebrowser' spawning /bin/sh for readiness probes
  • Ops running the filebrowser CLI (`filebrowser config`, `filebrowser users`) interactively from a shell where the parent/child order is inverted
  • Backup/maintenance scripts invoked by a filebrowser-named systemd unit that call uname/hostname
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"^\s*test\s" and not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alert — confirm InitiatingProcessFileName=='filebrowser' and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for injected recon (id/whoami/cat /etc/passwd) or separators; correlate to the host's web/reverse-proxy logs for a POST to /api/login in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host, stop the filebrowser container/service, and disable hook authentication (set auth.method back to json/proxy) or patch to filebrowser v2 > 2.63.5. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for follow-on egress/reverse shells (UC2), new files under the served directory (webshell/backdoor), new cron entries or SSH authorized_keys, and any outbound connection from the filebrowser process subtree.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where (FileName in~ ("id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php"))
    or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh")
        and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("/id","/whoami","/uname","/hostname","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/perl","/ruby","/php"))
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh")
        and (TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","whoami","uname","/dev/tcp/")
             or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @";|\|\||&&|\$\(|\x60"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File Browser hook-auth RCE follow-on: reverse shell / egress tooling under filebrowser (CVE-2026-54088) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the File Browser process subtree spawning a reverse shell or ingress/download tool after successful command injection. Distinct from the discovery UC: this targets the C2 stage where the injected command establishes an interactive shell (`bash -i`, `/dev/tcp/`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `mkfifo`) or pulls a second-stage payload (`curl`/`wget` piped to a shell) from the `filebrowser` process. Rationale: Pairs the concrete vulnerable parent binary `filebrowser` with high-specificity reverse-shell/ingress signatures (`/dev/tcp/`, `bash -i`, `nc -e`, `socat`, `curl|wget` piped to shell) from the RCE class described in the advisory. These command-line strings are near-zero-FP and map the exploit to its C2/second-stage phase. Corroborated via filebrowser.org auth docs and the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m93h-4hw7-5qcm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/master/auth/hook.go
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit hook-auth command that uses curl/wget to POST credentials to an external authentication API
  • filebrowser sidecar/init script that pulls config or TLS certs via curl/wget at startup
  • Admin debugging the container with `docker exec` where the shell's parent resolves to filebrowser
  • Monitoring agent invoking python from within the filebrowser service context for metrics
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://auth.","/certs/","/token") and ProcessCommandLine !has "/dev/tcp/" and ProcessCommandLine !has "| sh" and ProcessCommandLine !has "|sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the child ProcessCommandLine and resolve the destination host/port (grep for the IP after /dev/tcp/ or the nc/socat/curl target); check DeviceNetworkEvents on the same host for a matching outbound public connection in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the filebrowser process/container, block the observed C2 IP/domain at the egress firewall, and rotate any credentials/secrets readable by the filebrowser service account. 3) Hunt: search for downloaded second-stage files, persistence (cron, systemd units, authorized_keys), lateral SSH from this host, and repeat the UC1 discovery query to scope earlier recon.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "filebrowser"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh","ksh","nc","ncat","netcat","socat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "filebrowser" or ParentProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh","/ksh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","bash -i","sh -i","mkfifo","socat","import socket","import pty","curl ","wget ")
    or TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\bnc(\.traditional)?\b.*\s-[ec]\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser /api/login carrying forged X-Remote-User / X-Auth proxy-auth header AIExploitation High
Hunts POST requests to the FileBrowser /api/login endpoint that carry a proxy-auth identity header (e.g. X-Remote-User) but originate from a source other than the trusted reverse proxy. CVE-2026-54089 lets any client that reaches FileBrowser directly forge this header to be minted an admin JWT with no password check. Rationale: Anchors on the FileBrowser-specific /api/login API path (the endpoint that reaches ProxyAuth.Auth), surfacing source IP so an analyst can spot logins arriving from anything other than the reverse proxy. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory and the filebrowser auth/proxy.go source. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/main/auth/proxy.go • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?vendor=filebrowser
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SSO users authenticating through the reverse proxy (their src IP will be the proxy)
  • Health-check / uptime monitors hitting /api/login on a schedule
  • CI/CD or backup jobs that authenticate to FileBrowser via API
  • Load balancer synthetic probes originating from an internal VIP
  • Admin troubleshooting the login flow directly from the host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the source IP is the sanctioned reverse proxy (nginx/Traefik/Caddy/Apache). Any /api/login POST from a non-proxy IP on a proxy-auth deployment is suspect; inspect the raw request for an X-Remote-User / X-Auth header. 2) Contain: firewall the FileBrowser port so only the proxy IP can reach it (bind to 127.0.0.1), and rotate the JWT signing key to invalidate any forged admin tokens. 3) Hunt: enumerate all users in the FileBrowser DB for accounts created out-of-band and review /api/settings, /api/users and file-download activity from the offending source.

FileBrowser auto-provisioning abuse: burst of distinct usernames via forged proxy header AIInstallation Medium
Detects a burst of /api/login POSTs from a single source in a short window, indicating exploitation of CVE-2026-54089's account-creation primitive where a forged header naming a non-existent user causes FileBrowser to auto-create that account. Multiple new usernames from one client is high-confidence provisioning abuse. Rationale: The article states a non-existent username auto-creates an account with no opt-in; each forged login with a fresh username persists a new user. A 10-in-10-minutes burst from one source is a strong provisioning-abuse signal that clean SSO traffic never produces. Corroborated via the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/blob/main/auth/proxy.go
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A busy SSO proxy funnelling many real users' first-time logins through one proxy egress IP (mitigate by excluding the proxy IP)
  • Automated login/health probes retrying rapidly
  • A pentest or vulnerability scanner enumerating the endpoint
  • Mobile clients retrying auth on flaky networks
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the FileBrowser user DB (or app logs) and list accounts whose creation timestamp aligns with the burst window; the auto-created accounts carry LockPassword=true and default permissions. 2) Contain: delete the rogue accounts, restrict the FileBrowser port to the proxy, and rotate the JWT signing key. 3) Hunt: review what each new account did (file downloads, /api/settings changes) and check whether default permissions granted execute/create capabilities that were abused.

FileBrowser admin endpoint access from session lacking legitimate admin login AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts write/delete actions against FileBrowser admin-only endpoints (/api/settings, /api/users, /api/resources) grouped by source, to surface a client exercising admin capability obtained through the CVE-2026-54089 forged-header bypass rather than a genuine credentialed admin session. Rationale: The bypass mints an admin JWT, so post-exploit activity shows up as writes to FileBrowser's admin-only API paths named in the article's attack flow. Grouping by source lets an analyst separate the sanctioned proxy from a direct attacker. Cross-checked with the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm

Direct inbound connection to FileBrowser port bypassing the reverse proxy AIDelivery High
Detects inbound TCP connections to the exposed FileBrowser listener (example port 8085 from the advisory PoC) from public / non-proxy sources. A proxy-auth deployment should have all traffic fronted by the reverse proxy, so any direct external connection is the precondition for the CVE-2026-54089 header-forgery bypass. Rationale: The advisory PoC publishes the container on port 8085 (-p 8085:80) and states direct reachability is the sole exploit prerequisite; a proxy-auth deployment should see zero non-proxy inbound to that port. Operators should adjust the port to their published value. Corroborated with the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm
ATT&CKT1199 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The reverse proxy itself connecting to the backend (allowlist the proxy IP)
  • Local health checks / monitoring agents on the same host or subnet
  • Container orchestration probes (Kubernetes liveness/readiness) hitting the port
  • An admin deliberately connecting for debugging as noted in the advisory
  • Internal vulnerability scanners sweeping the port
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileBrowser deployment uses auth.method=proxy and identify whether the connecting source is the sanctioned reverse proxy; anything else reaching the port directly can forge auth. 2) Contain: rebind FileBrowser to 127.0.0.1 or firewall the port so only the proxy IP can connect, then rotate the JWT signing key. 3) Hunt: correlate the source IP with /api/login POSTs and admin-endpoint writes in the same window, and audit the user DB for auto-created accounts.
